translation: Arjuna said: O Supreme Person (Purushottama)! What is that Absolute Brahman? What is the nature of the inner self (Adhyatma)? What constitutes the real definition of action (Karma)? What is declared to be the material realm (Adhibhuta)? And what is said to be the cosmic domain (Adhidaiva)?

Who is the lord of sacrifice (Adhiyajna) within this physical body, O Madhusudana, and how does he reside here? Furthermore, how can those of disciplined mind maintain awareness of You at the critical moment of death?

The Blessed Lord said: The supreme, imperishable Reality is Brahman. Its functional presence within each individual body as the core witness is called the inner self (Adhyatma). And that creative, outbound energy and discharge (visargah) which initiates, builds, and sustains the life of all created entities is designated by the name of action (Karma).
simple_explanation: Krishna provides technical, precise definitions. Brahman is the immutable base of the universe. Adhyatma is the divine ray operating inside the biological machine. Karma is defined in its grand, cosmic sense: it is the total, creative discharge of natural forces that causes life to emerge from matter. This cuts down the narrow, medieval notion that Karma only refers to pouring butter into literal fire pits.

translation: The endlessly changing, perishable physical nature (ksharo bhavah) constitutes the material realm (Adhibhuta). The cosmic, solar life-force that animates nature (Purusha) represents the cosmic domain (Adhidaiva). And I alone, residing as the inner witness within this physical body, O best among embodied beings, am the Lord of all sacrifice (Adhiyajna).

He who casts off his physical body at the hour of death, with his mind focused exclusively upon My divine presence, exits straight into My transcendent being; there is absolutely no doubt about this cosmic truth.

Whatever object, person, or mental state a human being continuously dwells upon when he leaves his physical body at the end, to that very state does he inevitably go, O son of Kunti, because his mind was systematically saturated and shaped by that specific thought pattern throughout his life.
simple_explanation: This verse exposes the dangerous, lazy superstition that a person can live an unrighteous, chaotic life and then magically change his destiny by shouting a holy name on his deathbed. Your final thought is the mathematical sum of your daily lifestyle. If you spend your life chasing money or harboring family attachments, your final thought will inevitably latch onto those anxieties. To secure a divine exit, you must build divine habits daily.

translation: Therefore, anchor your mind upon Me at all times, and perform your duty by engaging in this battle (mam anusmara yudhya cha). With your mind and intellect completely dedicated to Me, you will undoubtedly ascend to Me alone.

Practicing constant meditation, with his mind completely integrated in Yoga and refusing to stray after external distractions, the practitioner who continuously reflects upon the radiant, Supreme Divine Person, O Partha, goes straight to Him.

He who meditates upon the Omniscient Seer (Kavim), the Ancient Ruler of the universe, who is subtler than the subtlest atom, the absolute Supporter of all existence, whose divine form is inconceivable to the lower mind, and who blazes like a golden sun far beyond the darkness of ignorance (tamasah parastat);

At the hour of death, with an unmoving mind, sustained by deep devotion and the precise strength of his lifelong yoga practice (yoga-balena), channeling his entire vital life-force (Prana) smoothly into the center between the eyebrows—he attains that radiant, Supreme Divine Person.

That goal which the scholars of the Veda call the Imperishable (Akshara), into which the self- controlled ascetics freed from attachment enter, and desiring which seekers practice the sacred vow of celibacy (Brahmacharya)—that supreme state I shall summarize for you with succinct clarity.

Firmly closing all the sensory gateways of the physical body, confining the thoughts securely within the chamber of the heart, channeling the vital life-current upward into the higher brain center (murdhni), completely anchored in deep yogic concentration (yoga-dharanam);

Vibrating and chanting the sacred, monosyllabic name of Brahman—Om—while maintaining steady awareness of My divine reality, he who exits the physical body in this manner reaches the absolute, supreme Destination.

To that Yogi who is permanently integrated, whose mind never wanders after any other material desires, and who remembers Me constantly day after day, O Partha, I am incredibly easy to reach (sulabhah).

Having once ascended into My supreme presence, these magnificent, expanded souls (Mahatmanah) who have conquered the highest perfection are never subjected to rebirth in this transient world, which is a structural reservoir of friction and suffering (dukhalyam) .

All the various evolutionary planes of existence within this manifest universe, from the highest realm of Brahma down to the lowest cosmic structures, are temporary and subject to cyclical return, O Arjuna! But upon reaching My absolute reality, O son of Kunti, rebirth is entirely eliminated.

Those cosmic seers who understand the true scale of time know that a single cosmic day of Brahma spans a vast period of one thousand Mahayugas (4.32 billion human years), and his cosmic night is of identical duration. They alone are the genuine knowers of cosmic day and night (aho-ratra-vidah).
simple_explanation: Krishna presents a stunning cosmic scale of time, demolishing the narrow, short-sighted timelines common in many medieval theological mythologies. The universe breathes in and out through colossal evolutionary eras. Matter aggregates during the Day of Brahma, and dissolves into space during his Night. The Yogi must look past these changing periods and anchor his mind in the absolute eternity beyond them.

translation: With the dawn of the cosmic day, all manifest entities and worlds stream out from the unmanifest primordial matter (Apyakta). And as the cosmic night closes in, they dissolve completely back into that very same unmanifest source.

This entire collective multitude of living creatures and material worlds (bhuta-gramah) helplessly emerges into visibility again and again with the arrival of the cosmic day, and dissolves away into invisibility with the arrival of the cosmic night, O Partha.

But standing far above and beyond this manifest and unmanifest primordial matter, there exists another, transcendent, eternal Unmanifest Reality (Sanatanah Avyakto Bhavah) which never perishes, even when all created entities and universes are utterly dissolved.

This transcendent Unmanifest Reality is designated by the title of the Imperishable (Akshara); the ancient sages declare It to be the absolute, highest Destination. Those who reach It never slide back into the friction of material rebirth; that represents My supreme, absolute State.

That Supreme Person (Purusha), within whom all living creatures reside and by whom this entire cosmos is pervaded, O Partha, can be reached exclusively through unswerving, single- minded devotion (ananyaya bhaktya).

I shall now explain to you, O foremost of the Bharata dynasty, the distinct metaphysical pathways (kalam) exiting along which at the time of death, Yogis achieve permanent liberation (anavrittim) or return once more to material rebirth (avrittim).

Fire, light, daytime, the bright fortnight of the waxing moon, and the six months of the sun's northern course (Uttarayanam)—exiting along this radiant path, those who possess knowledge of the Divine ascend directly to Brahman.
simple_explanation: Verses 24 and 25 utilize classical Vedic allegories (Devayana and Pitriyana, rooted in Chandogya Upanishad) to represent internal psychological states, rather than literal weather cycles or calendar dates. The elements of fire, day, and Uttarayana represent a mind exiting the body in full clarity, completely illuminated by wisdom, focus, and public-spirited alignment.

translation: Smoke, night, the dark fortnight of the waning moon, and the six months of the sun's southern course (Dakshinayanamp)—exiting along this dim pathway, the reward-driven practitioner reaches only the reflective, transient mental state (chandramasam jyotih) and is bound to return to birth.

These two pathways—the bright, radiant track (shukla) and the dark, smoky track (krishna)— are looked upon as the two permanent, structural choices available to the world. By selecting the first, a person wins liberation; by sliding into the second, he returns to the cycle of rebirth.

Knowing the precise architecture of these two pathways, O Partha, an enlightened Yogi is never deluded or misled by transient rewards. Therefore, O Arjuna, remain permanently anchored in Yoga at all moments of your life!

Understanding this profound science, the Yogi completely transcends all the superficial, material rewards allocated for the mechanical study of the Vedas, the performance of rituals, the practice of bodily austerities, and the giving of charity. He rises far above them all and ascends directly to the ancient, supreme, and absolute State of the Divine.
